title: WORD: Diffusion-Based Posterior Inference for Online Goal Recognition
claim: Ambiguous partial trajectories stay consistent with several goals, so a faithful observer must keep multiple hypotheses alive until later evidence disambiguates.
layout: single aerial photo panel, annotated overlay with colored goal stars and trajectory
description: A single full-width aerial drone photograph of a road intersection with the surroundings masked in black. Four colored stars mark candidate exits at the image edges, each with a gray label box: blue w0 at upper left, green w1 at right, red w2 at bottom, orange w3 at left. A blue dot with a short arrow showing heading sits near the upper middle. A solid black curve traces the observed path from the blue star w0 to the dot. A dashed black curve continues from the dot across the crosswalk toward the red w2 star, with the green w1 exit also nearby. The eye goes first to the bright dot and stars against the dark asphalt. There are no panels, equations or text apart from the goal labels.
caption: Online goal recognition at a real intersection (illustrative example). A pedestrian (blue dot, with an arrow indicating heading), assumed to be goal-directed, is partway along an observed trajectory (solid black) toward one of four candidate exits (colored stars); the unobserved future is dashed. At this point, the past path and the current heading remain consistent with two of the exits (green $w^1$, red $w^2$) so a faithful belief over the agent's goal must keep both alive until later observations rule one out.
abstract: Goal recognition is the task of inferring an agent's intended goal from its observed behavior. Most existing work focuses on high-level symbolic recognition, abstracting away the continuous motion through which agents reach their goal. Methods that do reason over continuous trajectories rely on an explicit dynamics model that is hard to acquire and rarely transfers across settings. Neither approach explicitly learns how agents move toward each candidate goal, limiting accuracy on ambiguous trajectory prefixes where such knowledge is most needed. We present WoRD (Waypoint Recognition with Diffusion), which uses a learned trajectory prior to infer the agent's goal from partial observations. At each step, WoRD runs one warm-started denoising chain per candidate goal, steers each chain toward the observed trajectory through a closed-form log-likelihood gradient, and reweights the resulting samples by Bayes' rule into a calibrated posterior over goals. We evaluate WoRD on simulated robot settings, pedestrian trajectories, and vehicle trajectories using four metrics targeting distinct failure modes. Across all three settings, the same inference procedure preserves calibrated multimodal beliefs through ambiguous prefixes where filter- and classifier-based observers collapse to a single mode or grow overconfident.
